[ABOUT KENYA NATIONAL BUREAU OF STATISTICS]

(i) Promoting co-ordination among producers, users and suppliers of official statistics by forming appropriate sector committees; and

( j)  Designating  statistics  produced  by  national statistical system as official statistics on being satisfied that the necessary criteria have been followed.

KNBS  has  an  elaborate  infrastructure  for  data collection  across  the  country.  This  includes,  a County Statistical Office in each of the 47 counties as data collection center, two sampling frames for implementation of censuses and surveys and various databases for socio-economic statistical information.

The Bureau collects various statistical information on monthly, quarterly, semi-annually and annual basis. Ad hoc surveys and studies are also carried out to gather information on specific indicators. Some of the statistical products of the Bureau include, Consumer Price Index (CPI), Leading Economic Indicators report, Quarterly Gross Domestic Product (GDP) release, Quarterly Producer Price Index (PPI), Quarterly Balance of Payment release, Annual Economic Survey report, Annual Statistical Abstract and County Statistical Abstract. The Bureau also provides information to local and international organizations including the IMF, World Bank, UN, COMESA, ILO and EAC; and other data users.

The Bureau maintains various platforms through which its products and statistical information are disseminated. The Bureau provides information for monitoring the country's development agenda as well as internationally agreed indicators such as the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

In undertaking its mandate, the Bureau is guided by the following Vision, Mission and Core Values.

text:
[Vision]

'Quality statistics for better lives'

[Mission]

'Provide, manage and promote quality statistics through utilization of best practices for public use'. Core Value and Principles

Professionalism: The Bureau shall maintain high standards while discharging its duties by abiding to professional considerations on the methods, standards and procedures in its work.

Integrity: The Bureau shall uphold high standards of integrity in all our dealings.

Confidentiality: The Bureau shall treat all information provided by stakeholders with strict confidentiality and use it exclusively for statistical purposes.

Customer Focus: The Bureau is committed to always place customers at the core of the Bureau business and ensure high quality of service at all times.

Innovation: The  Bureau  will  continuously  embrace creativity and innovation for value-addition in its business processes.

Teamwork: The Bureau shall uphold the team spirit in all our work and we shall endeavor to promote teamwork.

[Data Quality]

The Economic Survey report is an annual publication prepared by the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics that provides socio-economic information covering a five-year period. Statistics presented in Economic Survey reports are produced in line with internationally sound and scientific methods that are anchored on the fundamental principles of producing official statistics. In particular, the report presents information on all sectors of the economy based on the Kenya Standard Industrial classification of all Economic Activities (KESIC), as well as information on other emerging topical issues. Data quality is expressed in terms of dimensions in line with international best practices and recommendations, KNBS has adopted 11 key quality dimensions for assuring statistical quality:

Relevance: Implies the extent to which statistical data accurately  reflects  the  reality  of  the  population  or phenomena being studied. To ensure relevance in the Economic Survey, the Bureau has adhered to sound methodology  and  used  appropriate  data  collection techniques.

Accuracy: The degree of nearness that statistics have achieved in correctly representing the phenomena they measure. The Bureau ensures that the Economic Survey report is reliable, unbiased, and free from error for public good. This is expressed by: using established methods and procedures that have been tested and refined over time, undertaking rigorous quality control through verifying data sources, checking for inconsistencies, and conducting statistical tests.

Reliability: Refers to representing statistics free from errors and bias. Production of Economic Survey is based on  international  standards  and  methods.  Sampling and non-sampling errors that may occur are always disclosed. Data from administrative sources are subject to international best practices on statistics and are verified and validated through sectoral Technical Working Groups.

[Data Quality]

Reliability: Refers to representing statistics free from errors and bias. Production of Economic Survey is based on  international  standards  and  methods.  Sampling and non-sampling errors that may occur are always disclosed. Data from administrative sources are subject to international best practices on statistics and are verified and validated through sectoral Technical Working Groups.

Timeliness: The time lapse between data collection and receipt of the data for compilation and processing and data dissemination periods. The Economic Survey report is produced at most 150 days after the end of the review year. The report is therefore published annually.

Punctuality: The time lag between the actual delivery of the data and the target date when it should have been delivered. This relates to whether or not data are disseminated on scheduled release dates. The Bureau has put relevant mechanisms in place to ensure that the Economic Survey report is published annually by 30th April.

Accessibility: The ease and conditions under which statistical information can be obtained. The Economic Survey and other KNBS reports are disseminated through various  platforms.  The  platforms  include  the  KNBS website: www.knbs.or.ke, publications, press releases and social media among others. The hardcopy publication is also available at the KNBS library and county offices.

Clarity: The extent to which statistical information is presented in a clear, accessible, and easily understandable manner. Towards this, the Bureau has ensured that easily comprehensible metadata are available, and additional assistance is available to users to facilitate varied use of statistical information by a wide range of users.

Coherence: The adequacy of statistics to be combined in different ways and for different uses. It refers to comparisons between statistics for the same or largely

To ensure coherence in the Economic Survey Report, the Bureau has used standardized methodologies and definitions to ensure that data are comparable across different  sources  and  over  time.  Additionally,  data validation  was  sought  to  identify  outliers  or  other anomalies in the data.

Consistency: Refers to statistics having 'logical and  numerical  coherence.'  The  Bureau  maintains  a compendium of statistical definitions and has endeavored to provide the same format of statistical tables as in previous years to enable uniformity and trend comparison over time.

Methodological Soundness: Refers to the extent to which the methods used to collect, process, and analyze data are scientifically rigorous, transparent, and reliable. In compiling the Economic Survey report, the Bureau has adhered to internationally recognized standards and guidelines for statistical practice and professional standards enshrined in the UN Fundamental Principles for Official Statistics.

Integrity: Refers to values and related practices that maintain confidence in the eyes of users in the agency producing statistics and ultimately in the statistical product. Towards this, the Bureau adheres to ethical and professional standards that uphold transparency, accountability and methodological soundness in the production and dissemination of the Economic Survey Report.

[Data Sources]

The statistics published in the Economic Survey reports are  based  on  a  wide  variety  of  sources  including own  surveys  and  censuses,  studies  carried  out  by other institutions and administrative data collected by  Ministries,  Departments  and  Agencies,  County Governments, and establishments. The sources of data are always dully acknowledged.

[International Scene]

The global economy remained resilient in 2024 despite ongoing challenges such as high energy and food prices and tighter monetary policies. Global real GDP grew by 3.2 per cent in 2024 compared to 3.3 per cent in 2023. Advanced Economies maintained stable growth at 1.7 per cent, mainly supported by easing monetary policies, strong domestic demand, and investment. In contrast, Emerging Market and Developing Economies (EMDEs) experienced a decline in growth from 4.4 per cent in 2023 to 4.2 per cent in 2024, primarily due to disruptions in commodity production and shipping. In 2024, Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) real GDP grew by 3.8 per cent, while that of East African Community (EAC-5) region grew by 5.4 per cent, mainly driven by government spending, service sector productivity and regional trade.

[3.2%]

[3.8%]

Global inflation eased to 5.7 per cent in 2024 from 6.7  per  cent  in  2023,  largely  due  to  stabilizing commodity prices and improved labor supply, with inflation returning to target levels in many economies. However, some SSA countries, including Angola, Ethiopia, and Nigeria, continued to face double-digit inflation. Global trade rebounded, expanding by 3.4 per cent, supported by strong growth in business services, tourism, and recovery of consumption of goods from USA. Labour market conditions remained steady, with both the global unemployment rate and labor force participation rate unchanged at 5.0 per cent and 61.0 per cent respectively in both 2023 and 2024.

[Economic Performance]

In 2024, Kenya's real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by 4.7 per cent, compared to a revised growth of 5.7 per cent in 2023. The growth was noted in most of the sectors of the economy with Agriculture, Forestry and Fishing growing by 4.6 per cent compared to 6.6 per cent growth in 2023. Other sectors also had notable growths including Financial & Insurance Activities (7.6%), Transportation and Storage (4.4%) and  Real  Estate  (5.3%).  Construction  however, recorded a contraction of 0.7 per cent down from a growth of 3.0 per cent in 2023. Similarly, mining and quarrying recorded a contraction of 9.2 per cent compared to a 2023 contraction of 6.5 per cent as evidenced in the reduced production of key minerals, including construction materials, titanium, salt (crude), and gemstones.

In 2024, Kenya's real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by 4.7 per cent, compared to a revised growth of 5.7 per cent in 2023. The growth was noted in most of the sectors of the economy with Agriculture, Forestry and Fishing growing by 4.6 per cent compared to 6.6 per cent growth in 2023. Other sectors also had notable growths including Financial & Insurance Activities (7.6%), Transportation and Storage (4.4%) and  Real  Estate  (5.3%).  Construction  however, recorded a contraction of 0.7 per cent down from a growth of 3.0 per cent in 2023. Similarly, mining and quarrying recorded a contraction of 9.2 per cent compared to a 2023 contraction of 6.5 per cent as evidenced in the reduced production of key minerals, including construction materials, titanium, salt (crude), and gemstones.

Nominal GDP increased from KSh 15,033.6 billion in 2023 to KSh16,224.5 billion in 2024 out of which with Agriculture, Forestry and Fishing contributed 22.5 per cent, an increase from 21.5 per cent in 2023. Combined, service activities contributed 61.1 per cent of the GDP while industry-related activities comprised 16.5 per cent of the GDP in 2024. At current prices, the Gross National Disposable Income increased to KSh 16,997.9 billion in 2024 from KSh 15,752.9 billion in 2023. Consequently, the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) per capita increased from KSh 291,770 in 2023 to KSh 309,460 in 2024. The Private final consumption expenditure increased from KSh 11,460.0 billion in 2023 to KSh 12,483.7 billion in 2024 while the government final consumption expenditure increased to KSh 1,809.9 billion from KSh 1,770.5 billion in 2023.

[Employment, Earnings and Consumer Prices]

Employment in the modern and informal sectors, excluding small-scale agriculture, went up from 20.0 million in 2023 to 20.8 million in 2024. A total of 782.3 thousand new jobs were created in the economy in 2024. The modern sector created a total of 78.6 thousand jobs in 2024, reflecting a growth of 2.4 per cent. The informal sector created 703.7 thousand new jobs compared to 720.9 thousand in 2023, accounting for 90.0 per cent of all new jobs created, excluding small-scale agriculture.

In the private sector, wage employment registered a growth of 2.1 per cent in 2024 compared to 3.3 per cent in 2023. The leading industries in the private sector in 2024 providing the highest employment numbers  were  Manufacturing;  and  Agriculture, Forestry and Fishing, accounting for 15.9 per cent and 14.1 per cent, respectively. In the public sector, wage employment registered a growth of 3.1 per cent in 2024 compared to 5.9 per cent in 2023. Industries with the highest employment levels in the public sector were Education; and Public Administration and Defence; Compulsory Social Security, which accounted for 45.2 per cent and 34.4 per cent of total employment in the sector, respectively, in 2024.

[Employment, Earnings and Consumer Prices]

In the private sector, wage employment registered a growth of 2.1 per cent in 2024 compared to 3.3 per cent in 2023. The leading industries in the private sector in 2024 providing the highest employment numbers  were  Manufacturing;  and  Agriculture, Forestry and Fishing, accounting for 15.9 per cent and 14.1 per cent, respectively. In the public sector, wage employment registered a growth of 3.1 per cent in 2024 compared to 5.9 per cent in 2023. Industries with the highest employment levels in the public sector were Education; and Public Administration and Defence; Compulsory Social Security, which accounted for 45.2 per cent and 34.4 per cent of total employment in the sector, respectively, in 2024.

The nominal wage bill grew by 7.2 per cent to KSh 2,998.8 billion in 2024. The private sector wage bill expanded by 7.7 per cent to KSh 2,117.4 billion in 2024, while the public sector wage bill increased by 5.8 per cent to KSh 881.4 billion in 2024, accounting for 29.4 per cent of the total wage payments in 2024.

Overall  average  annual  earnings  increased  from KSh 894.2 thousand in 2023 to KSh 933.1 thousand in 2024. Overall, real annual average earnings per employee decreased from KSh 667.3 thousand in 2023 to KSh 665.4 thousand in 2024.

[Employment, Earnings and Consumer Prices]

Overall  average  annual  earnings  increased  from KSh 894.2 thousand in 2023 to KSh 933.1 thousand in 2024. Overall, real annual average earnings per employee decreased from KSh 667.3 thousand in 2023 to KSh 665.4 thousand in 2024.

The year-on-year inflation for 2024 eased to 4.5 per cent from 7.7 per cent in 2023. The inflation reported in 2024 was lowest in the last five years.

This was mainly due to the reduction food prices in the year under review. The annual average Consumer Price  Index  (CPI)  for  2024  stood  at  139.69.  The food and non-alcoholic beverages division inflation rate increased by 5.6 per cent in 2024, which was attributable to favorable weather conditions compared with 9.7 per cent in 2023.  In 2024, the transport index eased to 5.0 per cent compared to 12.2 per cent in 2023, mainly driven by the increase in prices of matatu and country bus fares, however, prices of diesel and petrol dropped.

In 2024, the transport index eased to 5.0 per cent compared to 12.2 per cent in 2023, mainly driven by the increase in prices of matatu and country bus fares, however, prices of diesel and petrol dropped.

In 2024, sugar, confectionery and desserts class for food and non-alcoholic beverages recorded a negative inflation rate of 10.7 per cent due to decline in prices of sugar. Prices of maize grain loose recorded the highest decrease of 19.3 per cent. Nairobi's lowerincome group recorded the lowest inflation of 4.2 per cent compared to other income segments in Nairobi. Effects of high exchange rates were felt at the beginning of the year in the Nairobi upper-income group and middle-income group, resulting in high prices of imported commodities, hence high inflation in the baskets of 4.8 per cent and 5.1 per cent in 2024, respectively.

[Money, Banking and Finance]

The Central Bank Rate (CBR) was lowered to 11.25 per cent as at December 2024 from 12.50 per cent in December 2023 as part of the Monetary policy measures by the regulator to support economic activity. Overall interest rates for commercial banks increased during the review period to 16.89 per cent. The 91-Day Treasury bill interest rate declined to 10.32 per cent in December 2024 from 15.70 per cent in December 2023. Further, the CBK's inter-bank rate reduced from 11.65 per cent in December 2023 to 11.45 per cent in December 2024. Broad Money supply (M3) grew by 1.0 per cent during the review period to stand at KSh 6,105.5 billion as at December 2024. Total exports rose from KSh 1,007.9 billion in 2023 to KSh 1,112.3 billion in 2024, largely driven by increased re-exports. Earnings from re-exports grew by 77.3 per cent to KSh 180.2 billion in 2024, primarily due to increased re-exports of kerosene type jet fuel. [Agriculture Sector]

The agriculture sector exhibited an overall improved performance in 2024, which was attributable to increased crop yields, increased livestock production coupled with increased government support to the sector. However, rainfall patterns varied across seasons as the March-May long rains were above average while October-December short rains were erratic and poorly distributed.  The Agriculture Value Added at constant prices increased from KSh 1,634.1 billion in 2023 to KSh 1,706.0 billion in 2024.

Maize production decreased by 6.1 per cent to 44.7 million bags in 2024 which was partly due to erratic short rains in 2024.  Abundant rainfall in tea growing areas resulted in a 4.2 per cent increase in green leaf

tea production to 2,687.2 thousand tonnes in 2024. Similarly, total milk production increased by 1.0 per cent to 5,334.8 million litres in 2024. Consequently, the quantity of marketed milk increased by 12.0 per cent to 908.4 million litres in 2024. However, the quantity of exported fresh horticultural produce declined by 14.1 per cent to 402.2 thousand tonnes in 2024. Sugar cane production increased by 68.7 per cent to 9.4 million tonnes in 2024. The production of coffee increased by 1.6 per cent to 49.5 thousand tonnes during the crop year under review.

Per caput caloric supply increased to 2,153.7 kcal/day in 2024 while Self-Sufficiency Ratio (SSR) improved to 105.5 per cent in 2024. In addition, the Import Dependency Ratio (IDR) dropped to 17.3 per cent in 204, indicating improved local food production.

The total expenditure on water supply and related services is expected to decline by 4.1 per cent to KSh 64.3 billion in 2024/25. KSh 9.8 billion in 2023/24 to KSh 11.5 billion in 2024/25. The number of boreholes drilled increased by 2.9 per cent to 47,199 in 2024/25, with the private sector accounting for the largest share.

The total quantity of fish landed increased by 4.4 per cent to 168.4 thousand tonnes in 2024, resulting to a 10.4 per cent increase to KSh 39.6 billion.

The net stocked plantation area increased from 144.8 thousand hectares in 2023 to 147.0 thousand hectares in 2024. New Area Planted more than doubled to 4.9 thousand hectares in 2024 from 2.4 thousand hectares in 2023. This is attributed to the Government's 'Jaza Miti' campaign of planting 15 billion trees by 2032.

[Manufacturing Sector]

In 2024, the manufacturing sector grew by 2.8 per cent, up from 2.2 per cent in 2023, contributing 7.3 per cent to the GDP. The volume of output increased by 4.4 per cent compared to 2.8 per cent the previous year. Formal manufacturing employment rose by 1.9 per cent to 369.2 thousand persons, with the sector accounting for 11.5 per cent of the share of formal employment.

Agro-based industries recorded growth of 9.8 per cent, largely driven by a rebound in sugar production, which rose by 72.5 per cent. Sugar experienced the steepest drop in average producer prices at 28.8 per cent, followed by maize flour at 21.5 per cent. Cement production declined from 9,616.1 to 8,852.6 thousand tonnes, similarly cement consumption and stocks declined from 9,195.9 to 8,537.0 thousand tonnes, in 2024.

The Producer Price Index (PPI) decreased to 139.04 in 2024, from 140.20 in 2023. [Construction Sector]

The construction sector declined by 0.7 per cent in 2024 compared to 3.0 per cent growth registered in 2023. The number of international visitor arrivals grew by  14.7  per  cent  to  2,394.4  thousand  in  2024. The improvement is mainly attributed to strategic interventions adopted during the year. In 2024, the number of accredited hotels stood at 904 of which 289 were gold rated, 317 silver rated and 298 bronze rated. During the year under review, hotel bed-nights occupancy grew by 18.9 per cent to 10,262.1 thousand in 2024. The number of international conferences went up by 2.3 per cent to 999 in 2024, while local conferences increased by 4.7 per cent to 11,225. The growth in both accommodation and conferences were largely supported by the increased visitor arrivals, hosting  of  high-profile  meetings  and  improved domestic market. Over the same period, the number of visitors to museums, snake parks and historical sites rose by 6.9 per cent to 1,152.7 thousand.

[2025 Economic Outlook]

The global economy is projected to remain stable and post an improved performance of 3.3 per cent in 2025. The projected growth is supported by easing global inflation and supply chain constraints, stronger performance in the United States and some large emerging market economies. The growth is further reinforced by improved labour market conditions, as nominal wage growth continues to show signs of moderation. However, projected global growth is  expected  to  be  uneven,  masking  significant differences across regions and countries. In advanced economies such as the USA, growth is underpinned by a robust demand reflecting strong wealth effects, easing monetary policy alongside improved financial market  conditions.  However,  in  the  euro  area, geopolitical tensions continue to weigh on growth prospects, partly due to heightened political and policy uncertainty. In other advanced economies, growth is supported by a recovery in real incomes and consumption patterns but likely hampered by uncertainty in trade policy. Growth is projected to remain stable and solid in China and India. In the Middle East and Central Asia, growth is projected to pick up in 2025 but at a slower pace. Growth in sub-Saharan Africa is expected to pick up in 2025 but expected to slow down in emerging and developing Europe.

Kenya's economy is projected to remain resilient and stable in 2025. The projected growth is expected to be driven by a strong services sector, enhanced agricultural productivity supported by favourable weather and distribution of subsidized fertilizer and seeds by the Government.

Kenya's economy is projected to remain resilient and stable in 2025. The projected growth is expected to be driven by a strong services sector, enhanced agricultural productivity supported by favourable weather and distribution  of  subsidized  fertilizer and seeds by the Government. The outlook is also underpinned by a stable macroeconomic environment and  steady  international  oil  prices.  Inflation  is projected to stay within the Government's target range of 2.5 per cent to 7.5 per cent, supported by low non-food-non-fuel inflation, lower food and energy prices, and a stable exchange rate. The decline in interest rates is expected to continue to support growth in  private  sector  credit,  boost  economic activity and accelerate growth.

Further, enhanced implementation of priority value chains under the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda in core areas of Agricultural Transformation; Micro, Small and Medium Enterprise (MSME) Economy; Housing and Settlement; Healthcare; and Digital Superhighway and Creative Economy- aided by the identified enablers- will accelerate inclusive growth, lower the cost of living; eradicate hunger; create jobs; expand the tax base; and improve foreign exchange balances. On the demand side, aggregate demand is expected to remain robust, supported by both public and private sector activity, stronger exports of goods and services, and sustained diaspora remittances.

The global economy remained resilient in 2024 despite ongoing challenges such as high energy and food prices and tighter monetary policies. World real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by 3.2 per cent in 2024, compared with 3.3 per cent growth recorded in 2023. The Advanced Economies seemed to catch up with the output levels projected before the pandemic while the Emerging Market and Developing Economies (EMDEs) were still bearing the scars of post COVID-19 pandemic as evidenced by a large output shortfall. The advanced Economies real GDP grew by 1.7 per cent in 2024, down from 1.8 per cent in 2023. This growth was mainly

1.6. In 2024, USA economy grew by 2.8 per cent, compared to 2.9 per cent growth recorded in 2023. The economy's growth was mainly supported by strong private consumption, increased investment in industrial sectors and government spending. [Euro Area]

1.7. The Euro Area registered real GDP growth of 0.8 per cent in 2024, an improvement from the 0.5 per cent growth recorded in 2023. The growth was mainly attributed to a rise in loan demand from businesses, coupled with a strong rebound in housing loans and other forms of lending to households. In 2024, inflation in the Euro Area was 2.4 per cent, a decline from 5.4 per cent in 2023. This easing was largely due to lower energy prices and reduced supply chain pressures. Unemployment in the bloc declined to 6.4 per cent in 2024 from 6.6 per cent in 2023. The current account surplus as a percentage of GDP widened from 2.7 per cent in 2023 to 3.7 per cent in 2024 driven by strong performance in goods and services trade.

[United Kingdom]

1.8. The United Kingdom's (UK) real GDP grew by 0.9 per cent in 2024, up from 0.3 per cent in 2023. This growth was largely attributed to an increase in retail sales volumes throughout the year and increased credit advanced to the private sector. Inflation eased from 7.3 per cent in 2023 to 2.6 per cent in 2024 partly due to the appreciation of the Sterling Pound and decline in global energy prices which helped offset pressure on imported inflation. The UK's unemployment rate rose from 4.0 per cent in 2023 to 4.2 per cent in 2024 while the current account balance as a percentage of GDP widened to a deficit of 2.8 per cent in 2024 from 2.0 per cent deficit in 2023.

[Japan]

1.9. Japan's real GDP in 2024 contracted by 0.3 per cent compared to 1.7 per cent growth in 2023. The contraction was largely due to structural constraints, supply chain disruptions, temporary supply disruption in the car industry and a slowdown in global demand. Inflation eased from 3.3 per cent in 2023 to 2.6 per cent in 2024, partly attributed to supportive fiscal measures such as energy subsidies and moderating food prices. Current account surplus as a percentage of GDP increased from 3.8 per cent in 2023 to 4.5 per cent in 2024 supported by a rebound in automobile and semiconductor-related exports, inbound tourism and improved manufacturing capacity.

[Germany]

1.10. In 2024, Germany's real GDP growth stood at 0.0 per cent rebounding from a contraction of 0.1 per cent in 2023, underpinned by the services sector. 1.14. The real GDP growth of India slowed to 6.8 per cent in 2024 from 8.2 per cent in 2023, supported by agriculture and service sectors. narrowed to 0.5 per cent in 2024 from 0.7 per cent in 2023 on account of increased service exports and remittance inflows.

1.15. Indonesia's real GDP growth in 2024 was 5.1 per cent compared to 5.0 per cent growth recorded in 2023, mainly driven by a recovery in domestic consumption and investment in infrastructure. silient with the real GDP expanding by 3.8 per cent in 2024 compared to 3.6 per cent growth in 2023. Burundi's economy slowed to 2.2 per cent in 2024 compared to 2.7 per cent growth in 2023, hindered by political uncertainties and limited investment inflows.

1.21. The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) recorded a slowed growth of 4.7 per cent in 2024 compared to 8.4 per cent growth in 2023 mainly attributed to fluctuation in commodity prices that impacted negatively the mining sector. The real GDP of South Sudan contracted by 26.4 per cent in 2024 compared to a 2.5 per cent growth in 2023 mainly due to internal conflicts disrupting oil production and exports.

[Southern African Development Community]

1.23. The Southern African Development Community (SADC) real GDP grew by 2.5 per cent in 2024 compared to 2.7 per cent growth in 2023. This slowdown was partly due to subdued economic activity in key member states, notably South Africa and Angola which were hit by drought, persistent power outages and terms of trade shocks. The region's inflation rose to 18.1 per cent in 2024, up from 16.9 per cent in 2023, driven by elevated food and energy prices, and currency depreciation in several countries in the bloc. Additionally, the current account deficit as a percentage of GDP widened to 2.6 per cent in 2024, from 2.3 per cent in 2023.

[West African Economic and Monetary Union]

1.24. The West African Economic and Monetary Union (WAEMU) experienced a robust economic performance in 2024, with real GDP growth accelerating to 6.2 per cent compared to 5.1 per cent growth in 2023. Infla -tion in the region eased to 3.2 per cent in 2024 from 3.8 per cent in 2023. This decline was largely due to the restrictive monetary policies implemented by the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO), which effectively curbed inflationary pressures. The current account deficit as a percentage of GDP narrowed to 6.3 per cent in 2024 from 9.7 per cent recorded in 2023. This positive trend was attributed to favourable developments in terms of trade, including a decline in the prices of imported energy products and an increase in prices of key exported commodities such as gold, cocoa, cotton, and rubber.

In 2024, the Economic and Monetary Community of Central Africa (CEMAC) experienced a modest economic recovery, with real GDP growth estimated at 3.7 per cent compared to 2.3 per cent growth in 2023. This improvement was primarily driven by a rebound in oil production and higher global commodity prices, which bolstered the economies of the member states such as Cameroon and Chad. Inflation in the region eased to 4.0 per cent in 2024, down from 5.4 per cent in 2023. This decline was largely due to continued tightening of monetary policy by Bank of Central African States' (BEAC)  which helped stabilise prices. The current account deficit as a percentage of GDP widened slightly from 0.4 per cent in 2023 to 0.6 per cent in 2024.

[Association of Southeast Asian Nations]

1.27. In 2024, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN-5) recorded a real GDP growth of 4.5 per cent, reflecting a slight improvement from the 4.0 per cent growth recorded in 2023. This growth was primarily driven by a moderate recovery in both domestic and external demand. Inflation across the region eased to 2.3 per cent in 2024 from 3.5 per cent in 2023, mainly due to the stabilization of global prices. The current account surplus as a percentage of GDP narrowed from 3.1 per cent in 2023 to 2.7 per cent in 2024 per cent primarily attributed to slower than expected global trade growth, particularly among major trading partners which impacted manufacturing exports from countries like Vietnam. However, economic performance varied across the individual member countries in 2024. Indonesia's real GDP grew by 5.1 per cent in 2024, while Malaysia saw a notable increase to 4.8 per cent in 2024 from 3.6 per cent growth recorded in 2023.   The Philippines economy recorded an expansion of 5.8 per cent, slightly higher than the 5.5 per cent growth recorded in 2023. In 2024, Thailand's economy grew at a more moderate pace of 2.8 per cent compared to 1.9 per cent growth in 2023. Vietnam recorded a growth of 6.1 per cent in 2024 compared to 5.0 per cent growth recorded in 2023.

[Maghreb]

1.28. In the Maghreb region, real GDP growth decelerated to 3.4 per cent in 2024 from 4.4 per cent in 2023, largely due to a decline in oil production and weak export performance. All the countries in the region recorded a slowed growth except Tunisia which recorded a real GDP growth of 1.6 per cent in 2024. Mauritania's real GDP expanded by 4.4 per cent in 2024 compared to an expansion of 6.5 per cent in 2023. Morocco's economy recorded a slowed growth of 2.8 per cent in 2024 compared to a growth of 3.4 per cent recorded in 2023, mainly propelled by a tourism rebound, strong manufacturing exports, and increased private consumption. Libya's economy sharply decelerated from 10.2 per cent in 2023 to 2.4 per cent during the review period due to reduced oil production and global demand. Similarly, Algeria's growth slowed to 3.8 per cent in 2024 from 4.1 per cent in 2023 due to global oil production cuts and subdued oil prices impacting overall economic growth. Inflation in the region dropped to 5.9 per cent in 2024 from 6.9 per cent in 2023, while the current account deficit as a percentage of GDP widened from 0.5 per cent in 2023 to 1.7 per cent in 2024. This was mainly attributed to adverse climatic conditions that negatively impacted agricultural production, leading to increased imports of cereals to meet domestic demand.

[Mashreq]

1.29. The Mashreq region registered a real GDP growth of 4.8 per cent in 2024, compared to 3.7 per cent in 2023, driven by a revival in industrial activity and sustained growth in the tourism sector. Inflation in the region declined to 17.8 per cent in 2024 from 22.8 per cent in 2023. The current account deficit as a percentage of GDP widened to 4.1 per cent in the reference period, from 3.9 per cent in 2023. Egypt recorded a decelerated real GDP growth of 2.7 per cent compared to 3.8 per cent in 2023, while Jordan registered a growth of 2.4 per cent slightly lower than 2.6 per cent recorded in 2023.

[Outlook]

1.30. The global economy is projected to remain stable at 3.3 per cent in 2025, maintaining the moderate pace observed in 2024. This indicates a degree of resilience despite major geopolitical and structural challenges, but also highlights the importance of maintaining cautious optimism amid persistent global risks. Advanced economies are expected to expand at a modest 1.9 per cent, constrained by fis -cal tightening and slowing consumer demand, while emerging markets and developing economies are set to grow by 4.2 per cent, driven by strong domestic demand, infrastructure development, and favourable demographic trends. The performance of countries among the advanced economies is projected to exhibit considerable diversity. The real GDP growth for USA is forecasted to slow down by 2.4 per cent, with the immigration policy anticipated to disrupt supply side and hence reduce potential output. The Euro Area, however, is expected to face a subdued growth of 1.3 per cent, limited by fiscal consolidation efforts and weak consumer confidence.

[Agriculture, Forestry and Fishing]

2.4. The Agriculture, Forestry and Fishing sector expanded by 4.6 per cent in 2024, compared to a growth of 6.6 per cent in 2023. The growth was largely a resultant of varied weather patterns during the year; with long rains being above-average while the short rains were below average, leading to mixed performance of the various crops. Production of maize, potatoes and millet declined while that of beans and sorghum increased. Maize production contracted by 6.1 per cent to 44.7 million bags in 2024 while potato production declined from 2.3 million tonnes to 2.2 million tonnes in 2024. On the other hand, beans production increased from 9.6 million bags in 2023 to 10.0 million bags in 2024.

2.5. During the review period, most cash crops recorded improved performances. Coffee production increased from 48.7 thousand tonnes in 2023 to 49.5 thousand tonnes in 2024, with earnings rising by 48.6 per cent to KSh 29.6 billion. Tea production rose by 4.9 per cent to 598.5 thousand tonnes in 2024. Cane production increased from 5.6 million tonnes in 2023 to 9.4 million tonnes in 2024. The performance of dairy subsector also improved, with the value of marketed milk increasing by 17.4 per cent in 2024 to KSh 60.0 billion, on account of a rise in milk deliveries from 810.8 million litres to 908.4 million litres over the same period.

On the other hand, fresh vegetable exports declined by more than half, from 164.1 thousand tonnes in 2023 to 74.3 thousand tonnes in 2024. Similarly, cut flower exports decreased by 11.9 per cent to 102.5 thousand tonnes in 2024 from 116.3 thousand tonnes in the previous year. The subsector's performance was affected by cargo delays at JKIA arising from Red Sea conflicts.

[Manufacturing]

2.7. The manufacturing sector expanded by 2.8 per cent in 2024 compared to 2.2 per cent growth in 2023. The growth was driven by a 4.6 per cent rise in the manufacture of food products, while manufacture of non-food products grew by 0.8 per cent. Growth in the food sub-sector was supported by increased processing of milk, which rose from 552.9 million litres in 2023 to 618.1 million litres in 2024. Sugar production increased from 472.8 thousand tonnes in 2023 to 815.5 thousand tonnes in 2024. Growth in beverage production was reinforced by a 15.6 per cent rise in soft drink production to 671.1 million litres in 2024 compared to 580.5 million litres in 2023. Processing of coffee and tea during the year grew by 7.8 and 4.9 per cent, respectively, in 2024.

2.8. In the non-food sub-sector, mixed performance was recorded across key activities. Production of galvanized sheets increased from 272.5 thousand tonnes in 2023 to 281.3 thousand tonnes in 2024. 2.8. In the non-food sub-sector, mixed performance was recorded across key activities. Production of galvanized sheets increased from 272.5 thousand tonnes in 2023 to 281.3 thousand tonnes in 2024. Similarly, production of textile and clothing, paper and paper products, pharmaceutical products and preparations and rubber and plastics products increased in the year

under review. On the other hand, cement production declined from 9,616.1 thousand tonnes in 2023 to 8,852.6 thousand tonnes in 2024. The number of assembled motor vehicles decreased by 14.6 per cent, from 13,527 in 2023 to 11,555 in 2024. Credit advanced to the manufacturing sector declined by 12.0 per cent, from KSh 639.4 billion in 2023 to KSh 562.9 billion in 2024. This decline was largely due to reduced lending from commercial banks, even as development finance institutions expanded their sup -port to manufacturing projects by 19.7 per cent to KSh 2.2 billion in 2024.

[Construction]

2.9. The construction sector contracted by 0.7 per cent in 2024 compared to 3.0 per cent growth in 2023. The contraction was reflected in the decline of key inputs such as cement and, iron and steel imports in the construction sector. Cement consumption declined from 9,195.8 thousand metric tonnes in 2023 to 8,537.0 thousand metric tonnes in 2024. Similarly, the volume of imported iron & steel and decreased by 8.9 per cent to stand at 1,101.1 thousand tonnes in 2024.In addition, the number of residential housing units completed by State Department for Housing (SDHUD) declined from 3,357 units in 2023 to 1,655 units in 2024. Credit advanced to enterprises in the construction sector declined from KSh 147.1 billion as at December 2023 to KSh 126.7 billion as at December 2024.

[Transportation and Storage]

2.10. Transportation and storage sector grew by 4.4 per cent in 2024 compared to a growth of 5.5 per cent in 2023. The growth was evidenced by increase in consumption of light diesel, increases in port throughput, air passenger traffic and freight transport via Metre Gauge Railway (MGR). Consumption of light diesel, a key input in land transport increased from 2,163.6 thousand metric tonnes in 2023 to 2,193.0 thousand metric tonnes in 2024. Total cargo throughput handled at the port of Mombasa grew by 13.9 per cent to 40,986 thousand metric tonnes in 2024. The total passenger air traffic increased from 12,205.8 thousand passengers in 2023 to 12,831.8 thousand in 2024. Similarly, the volume of freight transported via MGR rose marginally by 2.8 per cent to 1,029 thousand tonnes in 2024. However, passengers ferried via Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) declined from 2,729 thousand passengers in 2023 to 2,447 thousand passengers in 2024. Similarly, the volume of freight transported via SGR decreased slightly from 6,533 thousand tonnes in 2023 to 6,531 thousand tonnes in 2024.

[Electricity Supply]

2.11. Electricity supply posted a slowed growth of 1.9 per cent in 2024 compared to a growth of 3.1 per cent recorded in 2023. The growth was mainly attributed to increase in generation from hydro and decrease in generation of electricity from thermal sources. Total electricity generation increased by 0.5 per cent, to 12,569.3 Gigawatt Hour (GWh) in 2024 from 12,504.2 GWh in 2023.  Generation from hydro sources increased from 2,666.7 GWh in 2023 to 3,630.7 GWh in 2024; mainly supported by favourable rainfall conditions. Similarly, electricity generated via thermal declined by 13.5 per cent to 1,129.5 GWh in 2024. Electricity exports increased by 26.7 per cent to 42.8 GWh in 2024 while imports surged from 919.3 GWh in 2023 to 1,532 GWh in 2024.

2.12. However, electricity generated via geothermal which accounted for the highest proportion of total electricity generation at 44.2 per cent in 2024 declined by 8.0 per cent to stand at 5,551.0 GWh in 2024. Similarly, electricity generated via wind declined by 10.5 per cent to stand at 1,797.7 GWh, in 2024.

[Accommodation and Food Services]

2.13. Accommodation and Food Service activities sector recorded a growth of 25.7 per cent in 2024 compared to 33.6 per cent growth recorded in 2023. This growth was mainly driven by high-profile inter -national conferences and meetings held during the period under review. International visitor arrivals at the Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA) and Moi International Airport (MIA) rose by 12.1 per cent to stand at 1,832.8 thousand in 2024, up from 1,635.3 thousand in 2023. Notably, the number of hotel bed nights occupied increased by 18.9 per cent to 10,262.1 thousand in 2024 from 8,632.8 thousand recorded in 2023. The number of international conferences increased to 999 in 2024 from 977 in 2023, while local conferences increased by 4.7 per cent to 11,225 in 2024 from 10,725 in 2023, which further boosted its overall performance.

[Information and Communication]

2.14. The information and Communication sector recorded a decelerated growth of 7.0 per cent in the period under review compared to a growth of 10.3 per cent in 2023. The growth was mainly driven by mobile money and internet service activities. The number of mobile money transactions increased by 10.6 per cent to 2,681.9 in 2024 with the value increasing from KSh 7,954.0 billion in 2023 to KSh 8,697.7 billion in 2024. On voice call traffic, total domestic calls increased

by 16.9 per cent to 103.8 billion minutes in 2024. The total international outgoing telephone traffic increased by 3.2 per cent to 721.3 million minutes while the volume of international incoming telephone traffic rose by 58.5 per cent to 532.5 million minutes in 2024 from 335.9 million minutes in 2023.  The total utilised bandwidth increased from 11.0 million Mbps in 2023 to 13.4 billion Mbps in 2024, largely attributed to inclusion of satellite bandwidth during the year.

[Financial and Insurance Activities]

2.15. The financial and Insurance sector recorded a growth of 7.6 per cent in 2024 compared to 10.1 per cent growth in 2023. Broad Money supply (M3) expanded by 1.0 per cent from KSh 6,044.5 billion recorded in 2023 to KSh 6,105.5 billion in the year under review. Credit advanced to the national Government increased by 6.3 per cent to KSh 2,367.5 billion as at December 2024 while credit advanced to the private sector increased by 0.9 per cent to KSh 4,751.6 billion as at December 2024.

2.16. The insurance subsector grew by 16.3 per cent in 2024 compared to 12.2 per cent growth in 2023. Net premium from life insurance and general insurance increased by 20.9 per cent and 4.2 per cent to KSh 186.8 billion and KSh 138.4 billion, respectively, in 2024.

Economic Survey 2025

[Overview]

In the Financial Year 2023/24, the fiscal policy was designed to support the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA). This was implemented through a fiscal consolidation plan aimed at reducing the fiscal deficit, slow the growth of public debt and ensure effective implementation of debt management strategy, while providing essential public services. Strategies that were developed, included enhancing revenue collection by broadening the tax base and controlling overall expenditure. Implementation of the FY 2024/25 budget will however, be affected by the withdraw -al of the Finance Bill 2024, which was expected to generate additional revenue. To ensure the smooth execution of the FY 2024/25 budget and protect the fiscal consolidation plan, ministries, departments, agencies, and counties will prioritize and rationalize expenditures while safeguarding essential government programs.

The growth in exports was largely attributed to a 77.3 per cent surge in re-exports, while domestic exports recorded a 2.9 per cent increase. However, imports grew at a slower pace from KSh 2,612.0 billion in 2023 to KSh 2,706.3 billion in 2024. This resulted in an improved trade balance from a deficit of KSh 1,604.1 billion in 2023 to a deficit of KSh 1,594.0 billion in 2024.

6.11. Table 6.5 outlines the quantities of principal domestic exports from 2020 to 2024.  The quantities of most export commodities exhibited a decline in 2024. The drought severely affected the River Tana water flow which affected water intake in Bura irrigation scheme, leading to decreased acreages under production as well as the yields.

The Environment and Natural Resources sector plays a crucial role in Kenya's economic development,  providing  the  foundation  for key industries such as agriculture, tourism, and energy. In the face of climate change, population growth, and rapid urbanization, the management of these resources is vital for ensuring sustainable development and improving the quality of life for all Kenyans. The Government of Kenya (GoK)

In 2024, Kenya submitted its first Bi -ennial Transparency Report (BTR) under the Paris Agreement as required by the enhanced Transparency Framework.

8.29. The October-November-December (OND) 'Short Rains' season is a crucial rainfall period in Kenya, particularly for the Central and Eastern regions. October typically marks the onset of the short rains across many parts of the country, while November is generally the peak month of the season. December signals the cessation of the short rains, except in southern Kenya near the Tanzanian border, where rains normally persist for longer.

8.30. The predictability of the OND season is influenced  by  two  primary  climate  drivers:  the  El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD). However, forecasting Sea Surface Temperatures (SSTs) beyond the March-May period presents challenges due to the spring predictability barrier. As a result, it remains crucial to monitor updates issued by the meteorological department

for more accurate seasonal outlooks and potential changes in climatic conditions.

8.35. The MAM 2024 season marked the Long Rains periods that led to devastating floods, causing loss of lives, widespread destruction of crops, property, and livelihoods, displacement of populations and loss of livestock. The MAM 2024 started barely a few months into the recovery phase following the OND-2023 El Niño enhanced rainfall.

8.36. The enhanced MAM 2024 Long Rains resulted in flooding that impacted most parts of the country as predicted by the Kenya Meteorological Department (KMD). A total of 315 people died due to the floods, 58,641 households of which 293,205 individuals were displaced, and 412,263 persons were affect -ed. The flooding caused damage to roads, bridges, aerodromes, railway lines, school infrastructure, and health facilities where 298,673 acres of agricultural land and 9,367 livestock were washed away.

8.37. In the education sector, a total of 1,203 primary schools with a pupil population of 439,081 were affected, where 3,945 toilets were sunken, and 233 schools had their roofs blown off. At the same time, 294 secondary schools with a population of 124,358 students were affected, 941 toilets were sunken, and 81 schools had their roofs blown off. Over 48 schools hosted IDPs in various Counties affected by floods.

[Recent Developments]

8.41. The 29 th  United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP29) was held in Baku, Azerbaijan in November 2024. The conference, dubbed the 'Climate Finance COP,' emphasized the necessity for innovative and equitable funding mechanisms to bolster global adaptation and resilience efforts. The need for de -veloped nations to fulfill financial commitments to support developing countries was discussed, revealing a significant funding gap as only $250 billion is pledged annually against the $1.3 trillion required for climate action in developing nations. In response, the Government of Kenya (GoK) has actively mobilized both domestic and international resources to support climate mitigation and adaptation, implementing legislative frameworks and strategic partnerships to build climate resilience and transition towards a low-carbon economy.

8.42. The Financing Locally Led Climate Action (FLLoCA) Programme, implemented with support from the World Bank, focuses on performance-based funding to ensure accountability and impact. Additionally, the Climate Change Act (2016) established the Climate Change Fund, requiring counties to set up County Climate Change Funds (CCCFs) for investments in renewable energy, afforestation, and disaster risk management. Kenya has also embraced green financ -ing instruments, such as green bonds listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE), and is developing a carbon credit trading system to enhance private sector participation in climate action.

Kenya has also embraced green financ -ing instruments, such as green bonds listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE), and is developing a carbon credit trading system to enhance private sector participation in climate action.

8.43. To further boost climate finance, Kenya has secured funding from global institutions, including the Green Climate Fund (GCF), Adaptation Fund, and Climate Investment Funds (CIFs). The government is also promoting Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs) through organizations like KEPSA, attracting investments in clean energy, reforestation, and sustainable infrastructure. The National Climate Change Action Plan (NCCAP) serves as the guiding framework, aligning Kenya's climate investments with Vision 2030 and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), focusing on renewable energy expansion, climate-smart agriculture, and disaster risk management.

9.21. Environmental Economic Accounts are systems used to account for natural resource utilization. The accounts take stock of natural resources from extraction  to  intermediate  use  by  industries  to final use, to residuals/waste, which are eventually disposed of back to the environment. In addition, the  accounts  seek  to  promote  efficient  natural resource accounting and ensure a country can track how much it has utilized, estimate reserves in the environment, and promote proper disposal of residuals for  environmental  sustainability.  The  System  of Environmental Economic Accounts (SEEA) framework follows a similar accounting structure as the System of National Accounts (SNA). The concepts, definitions, and  classifications  used  in  SEEA  are  consistent with the 2008 SNA to facilitate the integration of environmental and economic statistics.

[Cybersecurity]

14.29. The number of cybersecurity advisories and reported online crime experienced significant changes in the period under review as shown in Table 14.15. The total cybersecurity advisories increased by 48.1 per cent to 39.0 million in 2024.   Malware advisories more than doubled from 1.1 million in 2023 to 2.5 million in 2024, while website application attack advisories more than tripled from about 3.9 million in 2023 to 13.6 million in 2024. Conversely, advisories related to system vulnerabilities declined by 11.3 per cent while those for botnet/DDoS attacks dropped by 28.0 per cent in 2024.  It is important to note that the reporting of digital investigation and digital forensics advisories was decommissioned in 2024 due to change of reporting of these crimes.

14.30. The total number of reported online crimes almost doubled to 3.5 billion in 2024. During the review period, two new categories of online crimes were reported. These were Brute force attacks which involve automated, systematic attempts to crack passwords or encryption by trying every possible combination until the correct one is found and mobile application attacks which target vulnerabilities in mobile apps to compromise user data or disrupt services. In 2024, 127.8 million Brute force attacks and 526.4 thousand mobile application attacks were reported.

[Konza Technopolis]

14.32. Konza Technopolis, the flagship smart city, stands as a key pillar in the country's journey towards becoming a knowledge-based economy. As one of the core enablers under BETA, specifically the Digital Superhighway pillar, Konza is not only a symbol of technological advancement but also a strategic platform for delivering innovation, generating high-value jobs and driving inclusive socio-economic transformation. The project is anchored on a robust blend of horizontal and vertical infrastructure. Horizontal infrastructure refers to the foundational, ground -level networks roads, utility corridors, water and sewer lines, power distribution, and fibre -optic duct while vertical infrastructure comprises the above ground structures such as office towers, data centres, residential blocks and mixed-use complexes. The key performing indicators for the Technopolis are intended to support evidence-based policymaking by informing data-driven decisions and enhancing transparency and accountability. Table 14.17 highlights selected indicators, which were identified based on Konza's strategic priorities and aligned with the intended outcomes of the Fourth Medium Term Plan (MTP IV).

[Overview]

The Government through the Ministry of Health is advancing digital health through robust policy frameworks such as the Kenya Digital Health Policy  (2020-2030)  and  the  Kenya  Health Information System (KHIS). These initiatives are designed to support interoperability and align with the broader goals of Universal Health Coverage (UHC). Leveraging on a range of technologies including mobile health (mHealth) applications, electronic health records (EHRs),

telemedicine, health information systems (HIS), and AI-powered diagnostic tools, Kenya is transforming the way healthcare is delivered. These platforms are bridging critical gaps in the health system, improving access to care in remote areas, addressing the shortage of healthcare professionals and enhancing efficiency of data collection and reporting.

thousand expected births in 2024. During the same period, registered deaths were 206,417 compared to 460,585 expected deaths, accounting for 44.8 per cent completeness in registration of deaths.

Source: Civil Registration Services

[Developments in the Health Sector Social Health Authority]

16.38. The Social Health Insurance (SHI) Act 2023 became operational in October 2023, repealing the NHIF Act of 1998. Consequently, the Social Health Authority (SHA) was established by the SHI Act 2023 to manage three primary funds, namely: Primary Health care (PHC) Fund, Social Health Insurance Fund (SHIF) and Emergency, Chronic and Critical Illness Fund to enhance healthcare financing in Kenya. The commencement date for the Act was 22 nd  November 2023, after gazettement by the Cabinet Secretary for Health, with a one-year transition which ended on 21 st  November 2024.

16.39. The Social Health Insurance (SHI) Act 2023 aims to: promote strategic purchasing of health care services; enhance the pooling of resources and risk based on  the principles of solidarity, equity and efficiency to guarantee access to health care services to all; provide a framework for improved health outcomes and financial protection; and realign health care systems, process and programs for responsiveness, reliability and sustainability of health care in Kenya. Social Health Insurance is guided by the principles of pooling financial resources and risks -everyone contributing the same proportion of their income, everyone getting a standard package of benefits and standard reimbursement to all types of facilities.

16.40. Registration of citizens to SHA began on 1 st July 2024 while the roll out was from 1 st  October 2024. Central to SHA is Taifa Care which denotes the whole Universal Health Coverage (UHC) journey that includes all the pillars that constitute delivery of quality health services to all Kenyans.

19.3. Previously,  the  CBK  generated  Non-Food Non-Fuel (NFNF) as a proxy measure of core infla -tion using Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) data. The NFNF was computed by excluding food, transport and energy components from the overall inflation. While this measure played a vital role in understanding underlying inflation dynamics, it be -came imperative to have an official comprehensive measure of core inflation for Kenya. This need was informed by the fact that CBK has been transitioning to Inflation Targeting monetary policy framework and recently officially adopted the framework in line with the White Paper on Modernization of the Monetary Policy Framework and Operations, July 2021. While

price stability remains the main objective, distinguishing between headline inflation and core/underlying inflation is not only crucial but also a standard practice under Inflation Targeting framework. The transition to inflation targeting among many countries including developing and low-income countries in Africa is partly driven by the drawbacks of targeting monetary aggregates and the rapid evolution of financial innovations.

19.4. The KNBS has been publishing headline inflation at the end of every month without disaggregating it into core and non-core inflation. In January 2025, the Bureau started publishing Core and Non-Core Inflation. Core inflation is a measure of inflation that excludes commodities in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) basket whose prices are highly volatile and is critical in informing monetary policy decisions since it captures persistent price developments consistent with macroeconomic fundamentals. Specifically, core inflation provides an indi -cation of demand side pressures. Prices of the excluded components (non-core) are often driven by transient or supply-side factors such as seasonal weather conditions and international oil prices.

[Core and Non-Core Inflations]

19.5. Core inflation is a measure of inflation that is com -piled from products whose prices are non-volatile such as manufactured food items, health services, education services and ICT. The concept of core inflation is to re -move most or all the products whose prices are highly volatile or transient from the overall index since they cause distortions to the overall index. By removing such products from the index, it is argued that the remaining, less volatile index, better demonstrates the fundamental changes in the rate of inflation. It can thus be used for economic analysis and, indeed, economic policy decisions, particularly by the Central Bank whose primary objective is to ensure price stability.

19.6. Non-core inflation on the other hand is a measure that is compiled from products whose prices are volatile such as fresh vegetables, fresh milk, electricity, petrol, diesel, kerosene and bus fares. Prices of these commodities are influenced by supply-side factors such as seasonal weather patterns and fluctuations in inter -national oil prices.

[Methods of Computing Core Inflation Measures]

19.7. Literature identifies three main approaches to core inflation computation: exclusion method, statis -tical methods (including trimmed mean and weighted median among others) and model-based approach. 19.8. The statistical approach includes two main methods: trimmed mean and weighted median. The trimmed mean excludes extreme price changes (outliers) at a 10 per cent rate. The weighted median approach (50% trim) measures core inflation by focusing on the price change at the 50 th  percentile of the monthly distribution, aiming to capture central price changes and mitigate the impact of large fluctuations. However, the trimmed mean method requires some technical consideration:

(i) whether the trim will be symmetric or asymmetric;

(ii) choice of frequency of price changes;

(iii) seasonality; and

(iv) treatment of large expenditure items such as housing with large weights in the CPI.

19.9. Frequent changes in technical decisions can lead to reputation and communication challenges for the Central Bank, as they impact core inflation measures. The

model-based approach employs a common component method to determine core inflation using dynamic factor models from the CPI basket. This approach is rarely used by central banks, but literature shows that the US Federal Reserve and Bank of Canada employ factor models for alternative core inflation measures. The effectiveness of these measures for monetary policy relies on how well they enhance the transparency and accountability of the central bank.

19.10. The EAC Guidelines for Compiling Harmonized Consumer Price Indices (HCPI), March 2022 recommends exclusion of all items under the following broad categories in the computation of core indices: fresh fruits; fresh vegetables; fresh milk; dried vegetables; tobacco leaves; imported fuels (e.g., petrol, diesel, paraffin, and cooking gas etc.); solid fuels (e.g., charcoal, firewood etc.); and utilities (electricity, metered water, and unmetered water). Table 19.1 list the products under Classification of Individual Consumption by Purpose (COICOP 2018) recommended for exclusion in the core basket.
heading_path: Methods of Computing Core Inflation Measures

text:
[Selection of the Core and Non-Core Baskets and Weights]

19.11. The process of computing a core inflation measure for Kenya followed a two-step procedure. In the first step, the EAC guidelines for computation of harmonized CPIs for the EAC countries were used to identify the items to be excluded. This generated an initial core CPI basket of 280 items with a weight of 83.1 per cent. However, in addition to the list of recommended products, each EAC Partner State is supposed to determine additional CPI items to be excluded during the computation of the core index, based on measures of persistence and volatility of monthly consumer prices. Therefore, in the second step, robust statistical methods of assessing volatility such as standard deviations were applied to determine additional items in the CPI basket to be included/ excluded from the computation of the core inflation basket. Thus, the commodity indices were subjected to these statistical measures and a selection criterion was determined whereby commodities with a standard deviation above 25 were considered volatile and were excluded from the core CPI basket. For robustness, the standard deviations were computed over

different time periods, while excluding outlier years that were characterized with severe shocks such as COVID-19 pandemic and drought. Consequently, using historical trends, standard deviations and coefficient of variations, five additional items were identified and excluded in the computation of core inflation for Kenya. Therefore, the total core CPI basket constitutes 275 items and has a weight of 81.1 per cent. This is a more representative basket for the computation of core inflation compared with NFNF proxy measure of core inflation previously computed by CBK.

text:
[Core Basket and Weights]

19.12. To calculate the core inflation, a core CPI sub-basket is derived from the elementary CPI dataset of 330 items that is used in computing the headline CPI. After generation of the core CPI sub-basket, core inflation is then calculated based on annual, monthly or quarterly changes in the sub-basket index. The share of the core CPI sub-basket is 81.1 per cent as presented in Table 19.2.

19.13. The proxy for core inflation previ -ously used by the CBK, i.e. the NFNF inflation, had 200 items which constitutes 53.4 per cent of the overall CPI basket. Hence, the new measure of core inflation constitutes a larger share of the overall CPI basket and thus, provides a better capture of inflation dynamics.

[Non-Core Basket and Weights]

19.14. The non-core CPI index comprises goods and services whose prices are susceptible to short-term shocks and are, therefore, volatile. It is computed from the elementary goods and services items excluded from the CPI basket in the computation of the core index bringing the total number of items in the non-core index to 55. These items constitute a weight of 18.9 per cent of the overall CPI basket as presented in Table 19.3.

[Sub-Categories of the Non-Core Index]

19.15. The non-core CPI items fall under the following three sub-categories: Food Crops and Related Items; Energy, Fuels and Utilities and Transport.

[Food Crops and Related Items]

19.16. These commodities mainly comprise unprocessed food items, both vegetables and non-vegetables. The items are derived from the Food and Non-Alcoholic Beverages category of the CPI basket and constitute 11.7 per cent out of the 32.9 per cent weight of this category as shown in Table 19.4.

[Energy, Fuels and Utilities]

19.17. This sub-category comprises fuel items (petrol, diesel, kerosene), other energy items (firewood, char -coal, and liquefied petroleum gas/LPG), and utilities (electricity and water) as presented in Table 19.5. The items in this sub-category are obtained from Division 5 and 7, broad categories of COICOP: Housing, Water, Electricity, Gases and Other Fuels and Transport, re-

spectively. Items obtained from Division 5 comprise of electricity, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), kerosene/ paraffin, firewood, charcoal, water from water service providers, and water from vendors while items obtained from Division 7 comprise of petrol and diesel. Items obtained from Division 5 constitute 4.9 per cent out of the 14.6 per cent weight of this category while those obtained from Division 7 constitute 1.3 per cent out of the 9.6 per cent weight of this category.

[Transport]

19.18. The non-core items under this category comprises two items, namely country bus fares and local flights as presented in Table 6.

[Computation of the core and non-core inflation]

19.19. Computation of core and non-core inflation follows the same procedure used in computation of the headline inflation. First, lower-level indices in particular Elementary Aggregate Indices are computed using Jevons (geometric mean) method and secondly higher-level indices are computed.

[Overview]

This  section  provides  highlights  of  the 2023/24  Kenya  Housing  Survey  (KHS). The Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS)  conducted  the  2023/24  KHS  to update statistics on housing and residential dwellings in Kenya necessary for informing housing  sector  policies,  compilation  of national accounts statistics and international comparisons. Given that

PAGE 517

the last National Housing Survey was conducted in 2012, it was imperative to undertake a new survey to update the data on housing and fill data gaps necessary for periodic monitoring of the sector. The survey findings are thus instrumental for policy making, particularly in advancing the Affordable Housing  Program  (AHP)  under  Kenya's  BottomUp Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA) and tracking progress towards housing-related Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

20.2. Survey Objectives: The primary objective of the 2023/24 Kenya Housing Survey was to provide up-to-date statistics on housing in Kenya to inform policy formulation. The specific objectives of the survey were to:

Assess the quality and condition of housing units.

Evaluate the level of access to infrastructure and services

Evaluate housing affordability by providing insights into housing costs and rent.

Assess the level of awareness and perceptions regarding the Affordable Housing Program, housing regulations, and comfort in dwellings.

Track progress towards national housing goals (Vision 2030 and (SDG) 1, 5, 6, 7, 9, 11, 16 and 17 indicators related to housing).

Assess the change in land consumption using geospatial tools from 2016 to 2023.

[Overview]

Assess the change in land consumption using geospatial tools from 2016 to 2023.

20.3. Survey Design and Scope: The survey employed a cross-sectional study design to collect data for estimating housing indicators at national, rural, urban and county levels. To achieve this, a hybrid data collection system was incorporated, targeting both households and institutions. The household component of the survey was designed independently from that of the institutions. A sample survey was conducted for the households, while a census was carried out for all identified institutions key in the housing sector. The survey covered all the 47 counties to ensure that the coverage was comprehensive and representative of the entire country. The household component targeted residential housing units in both urban and rural areas while the institutional component targeted housing developers, real estate firms, Water Service Providers, County GovernmentsPhysical Planning Departments, National Environment Management Authority (NEMA) and Land Administration Department. The professional component targeted members from Engineers Board of Kenya (EBK), Kenya Institute of Planners (KIPs) and Board of Registration of Architects and Quantity Surveyors (BORAQS).

Sample  Selection: The  sample  for  the household component of the survey was drawn from the Kenya Household Master Sample Frame (K-HMSF), which was developed based on the 2019 Kenya Population and Housing Census. A total of 1,295 clusters were randomly selected from the sampling  frame  and  25,900  households  within these clusters were selected for interviews. The institutional component of the survey was conducted using multiple lists obtained from various sources, including the State Department for Housing and Urban Development and Water Service Regulatory Board. Emerging Issues

[Overview]

The real estate sector is a fundamental driver of economic growth. Its indicators play a pivotal role in informing housing sector planning, financial stability and economic policy formulation. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) identifies the real estate market as an important source of indicators relevant for both financial and non-financial sectors. In particular, the real estate index is used as a deflator in the balance sheet and fixed capital formation in the compilation of national accounts statistics. Further, residential property prices are a key indicator in measuring growth as they reflect the affordability of residen -tial units by households, either through ownership or rental arrangements.

20.23 .Commercial properties, on the other hand, provide economic agents with space for business operations and are mainly categorized by form of usage which includes office space/proper -ty, retail space/property, industrial property such as, warehousing and storage, factories among others. Whereas the Consumer Price Index (CPI) captures information on monthly rent, the current housing market supply side data was missing, necessitating the carrying out of the 2023/24 Real  Estate  Survey to provide indicators on property p r i c e s a n d rent  as well as demand and supply side indicators.

[Design and Methodology]

20.24. Survey objective: The overall objective of the 2023/24 Real Estate Survey was to collect data on prices for both residential and commercial properties. The specific ob -jectives were to provide; up-to-date market statistics on the real estate sector, information on trends in typologies for housing, information on prices and rent for residential and commercial properties and update the statistical business register

(SBR) for the sector.

20.25. Scope and target population: The 2023/24 Real Estate Survey targeted all establishments engaged in real estate activities drawn from (SBR). The classification was based on the Kenya Standard Indus -trial Classification of all Economic Activities (KeSIC) used to classify economic entities (units) according to activities in which they are engaged in. The real estate activities covered in the survey were real estate activities with own or leased property. This included buying and selling of residential and non-residential buildings; renting and operating of real estate; operating of furnished/serviced apartments, and activities of real estate developers of own property for leasing or sale (construction work done by a separate entity at a fee).

20.26. The survey also covered real estate activities on a fee or contract basis such as activities of real estate agents and brokers; intermediation in buying, selling and renting of real estate; and management of real estate. The survey collected information from institutions engaged in all real estate activities including real estate agents, property managers as well as developers. To supplement survey data, secondary data on real estate properties sold was obtained from real estate establishments and agents.

[Design and Methodology]

The survey also covered real estate activities on a fee or contract basis such as activities of real estate agents and brokers; intermediation in buying, selling and renting of real estate; and management of real estate. The survey collected information from institutions engaged in all real estate activities including real estate agents, property managers as well as developers. To supplement survey data, secondary data on real estate properties sold was obtained from real estate establishments and agents.

20.27. Reference period: The 2023/24 Real Estate Survey collected information for real estate properties that were on offer for sale, rent, sold and rented out/leased in 2023. In this regard, information was collected for properties that were advertised for sale/ let before 2023 and were still on offer for sale/let in 2023; properties advertised forsale/let before 2023 and were sold/ let during 2023, properties that were advertised for sale/ let in 2023 and were actually sold/ let in 2023; and properties that were advertised for sale/let in 2023 but were not sold during 2023.

[Survey Findings]

20.28. Legal Status of real estate firms: Figure 20.9 presents the legal status of firms engaged in real estate activities that were covered in the survey. The survey findings show 84.9 per cent of real estate firms were registered as local private limited companies, 4.0 per cent as sole proprietors and 4.5 per cent as local public limited companies. Real estate companies registered as partnerships were 5.0 per cent while 1.5 per cent of firms were registered as foreign private limited companies.

Legal Status of Real Estate Firm

20.29. Registration of real estate firms with profes -sional and regulatory institutions ensures professionalism, discipline and consumer protection among players in the sector. Out of the firms that took part in the survey, 52.9 per cent were registered with at least one professional or regulatory body in the country. Among the registered firms, 88.1 per cent were registered with the Estate Agents Registration Board, 40.7 per cent were registered with Valuers Registration Board (VRB) while 33.9 per cent were registered with Kenya Valuers and Estate Agents as shown in Figure 20.10.

In the properties market, real estate firms/ agents can provide housing financing arrangements/assistance to potential buyers of their property to encourage uptake of properties in the market through encouraging potential clients to purchase or rent their property.

The survey sought to establish if real estate firms provide such housing financing arrangements. The results in Figure 20.11 indicate that only 9.9 per cent of the real estate firms covered in the survey provide housing financing arrangements for buyers or renters of their property.

20.32. Figure 20.13 shows distribution of residential properties by type of amenities. Majority of residential properties (73.9 per cent) that were in the market had parking lots while 22.7 per cent had Domestic Servant

20.34. Table 20.9 presents average sale price of residential property by typology. The prices were informed by location, unique characteristics of properties such as number of bedrooms, gross floor ar -eas, land size of stand-alone units, floor area of flats and apartments. Other attributes which influenced property prices include environmental factors, safety levels and existing physical and social infrastructure such as sewerage and drainage systems, roads, public transport, health centre, education centre, and other social services. The average sale prices for residential properties were determined through weighting the prices based on the number of properties of similar characteristics per region to remove the random noise in the prices across regions.

20.35 . The national average sale price for a two, three and four bedroom and above bungalow was KSh 14.1, KSh 19.5 and KSh 49.9 million, respectively, in 2023. The sale price of a three-bedroom maisonette was KSh 20.9 million while that of a three-bedroom apartment and townhouse was KSh 12.4 million and KSh 17.3 million, respectively.
