Economic Survey 2025

[Overview]

The Kenya National Bureau of Statistics in collaboration with the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK), Financial Sector Deepening Trust (FSD) Kenya, and other public-private sector stakeholders carried out the 2024 FinAccess Household Survey between July and October 2024, with the report on top line findings launched on December 3 rd , 2024. This survey has been carried out every 2-3 years since 2006 with an objective of enhancing financial inclusion measurement and provide indicators to track progress in financial inclusion in Kenya. The 2024 Survey is unique in several

PAGE 541

ways. First, it provides the first data point for time series analysis of the change in financial inclusion at the county level. The findings at county level highlight the heterogeneity of the financial inclusion landscape. Secondly,  the  questionnaire  was  expanded  to improve the measurement of the four dimensions of financial inclusion: Access, Usage, Quality and Impact. Emerging issues such as sustainable finance (green finance), financial health, Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs), Agriculture, and Persons with Disabilities (PWDs) were also covered. This chapter presents highlights from the 2024 FinAccess Household Survey report which is available on the FinAccess portal on the KNBS website.

[Survey Objectives]

21.2. The main objective of FinAccess Household Surveys is to monitor developments and progress achieved  in  financial  inclusion.  It  also  enables policy makers and industry players to gain a better understanding and dynamics of Kenya's financial inclusion landscape. The specific survey objectives were:

Tracking  trends  and  progress  on  financial inclusion.

Providing information on barriers to financial inclusion.

Providing information on market conditions and opportunities.

Providing  data  for  academic  research  on financial inclusion.

[Survey Methodology]

21.3. The 2024 FinAccess Household Survey was a cross-sectional survey that targeted individuals aged 16 years and above residing in conventional households in Kenya. However, the report is based on analysis of data for individuals aged 18 years and above, as national identity cards, which is a key requirement to accessing formal financial services, only issued upon attaining this age. The survey sample was drawn from the Kenya Household Master Sample Frame (K-HMSF), which was developed based on the 2019 Kenya Population and Housing Census. The sample was designed to provide estimates at national as well as rural and urban areas, and across the fortyseven (47) counties. The minimum sample size was computed for each of the survey domains, resulting in a total sample size of 28,275 households and 1,885 Enumeration Areas (EAs). The survey results achieved 84.6 per cent response rate.

[Key Findings Classification of Financial Services and Products]

21.4. Financial services and products were classified according  to  the  most  frequently  used  formal financial service provider. Respondents who used at least one formal financial service provider were classified  as  formally  included.  Formal  financial service providers include banks, Savings and Credit Cooperatives (SACCOs), mobile phone financial service providers (MFSs) and insurance companies, among other providers. Respondents who did not use any formal provider but used at least one informal service provider (e.g. groups, chamas, shopkeeper credit, etc.) were classified as informally included. Respondents who did not use any formal or informal service providers were classified as financially excluded. The excluded population comprises of those that relied on basic financial mechanisms such as saving in secret/ hiding places or borrowing from a family member or a friend in case of a need.
heading_path: Key Findings Classification of Financial Services and Products

text:
[Overall Financial Access]

21.5. Overall access to formal financial services has seen a substantial increase, expanding from the baseline of 26.7 per cent in 2006 to 84.8 per cent in 2024 (Figure 21.1). This growth is on account of financial technology and innovations, especially in mobile money, and physical expansion as formal financial services providers take services closer to the population. This was also supported by a conducive regulatory environment and various Government initiatives toward an inclusive financial system.

21.6. The survey findings show that financial exclusion has decreased by 1.7 percentage points to 9.9 per cent in 2024, mainly on account of an increase in informal utilization of financial services.

[Financial Access by Products]

21.7. Access to various financial products and ser -vices in 2024 and 2021 are presented in Figure 21.2. Access to banking services increased to 52.5 per cent in 2024 from 44.1 per cent in 2021. The 'Used to use' cases increased between 2021 and 2024, with loss of income and cost of financial services being cited as the main reasons. 'Never used' cases cited affordability, relevance and awareness as limitations to access. The main reason for 'Never Used' of mobile money was due to lack of a mobile phone and eligibility due to lack of Identity cards.

8

[Financial Exclusion by Age Group and Residence]

21.8. The survey results indicated that 45.6 per cent of young people aged 18-25 in rural areas were formally excluded. Similarly, 12.4 per cent of older people aged 55 and above in rural areas were finan -cially excluded compared with 1.5 per cent of their counterparts in urban areas as shown in (Figure 21.3). The lack of national Identification Cards (IDs) among young people aged 18-25 largely explains the high exclusion rate.
heading_path: Financial Exclusion by Age Group and Residence

text:
[Financial Access by Sex]

21.9. Access to formal financial services and products between the female and male population narrowed to 1.6 percentage points in 2024 from 4.2 percentage points in 2021. This was a result of continued low uptake by male and increased access by female to 84.1 per cent in 2024 from 81.7 per cent in 2021 as shown in Figure 21.4.

[Formal Financial Access by Residence]

21.10. Urban population recorded the highest access to formal financial services and products through formal financial providers at 91.3 per cent compared to 80.2 per cent for the rural population as shown in Figure 21.5. The rural-urban gap in access to formal financial services providers continued to narrow on account of continued penetration of formal financial services providers through digital channels and physical channels like branches and agents.

[Financial Access by County]

21.11. Kiambu county had the highest formal financial inclusion at 94.0 per cent, while West Pokot County had the lowest formal financial inclusion at 48.5 per cent as shown in Table 21.1.  On the other hand, Turkana County had the highest level of exclusion at 31.5 per cent as shown in Table 21.2.

[Usage of Financial Services and Products by Provider]

21.12. The 2024 FinAccess Survey highlights shifting financial preferences in Kenya, with mobile money usage rising to 82.3 per cent in 2024 from 79.4 per cent in 2019. This is driven by expanded services, improved infrastructure, and greater adoption for Government services and e-commerce. Bank usage increased to 52.5 per cent, supported by infrastructure development. SACCOs participation grew to 11.7 per cent, reflecting broader reach, while informal group membership rose to 30.8 per cent, emphasizing the continued importance of grassroots financial systems. Investments in securities increased to 3.1 percent, boosted by new applications (apps) and higher returns, showcasing diverse consumer financial needs. In contrast, insurance uptake saw a slight decline to 22.0 per cent (Figure 21.6).
heading_path: Usage of Financial Services and Products by Provider

text:
[Usage by the Portfolio of Financial Services]

21.13. The survey findings indicate that consumers are transitioning from using a single service to using many services. The number of respondents who use two or more types of financial services and products increased to 79.7 per cent in 2024 from 75.3 per cent in 2021 (Figure 21.7). This reflects the increasing complexity of financial needs, which require a range of financial products and services to address them. However, the marginal decline in non-usage to 9.9 per cent suggests that some segments, particularly those without national IDs, still face barriers to accessing financial services.
heading_path: Usage by the Portfolio of Financial Services

text:
[Traditional Banking and Mobile Bank Usage]

21.14. The overall usage of traditional banking (Banking operations through physical branch networks) increased from 23.8 per cent in 2021 to 29.0 per cent in 2024 as shown in Figure 21.8.  However, the overall usage of mobile banking slightly decreased to 32.6 per cent in 2024 from 34.4 per cent in 2021(Figure 21.9).
heading_path: Traditional Banking and Mobile Bank Usage

text:
[The Financial Inclusion Fund (The Hustler Fund)]

21.15. The usage of Hustler Fund loan services for the urban population was 35.4 per cent while the rural population usage was 24.2 per cent. Usage of the fund among the male population was 31.8 per cent while female population usage was at 26.1 per cent. Usage of Hustler Fund by wealth quintiles indicates that 35.8 per cent of those in the highest wealth quintile use Hustler Fund, while 18.7 per cent of those in the lowest wealth quintile use Hustler Fund (Figure 21.10).
heading_path: The Financial Inclusion Fund (The Hustler Fund)

text:
[Insurance, Pensions and Investments Usage]

21.16. The survey findings show that usage of NSSF and investments increased in 2024 to 11.4 per cent and 3.1 per cent, respectively. However, the overall usage of NHIF declined during the period to 19.4 per cent as shown in Figure 21.11.

[a) Knowledge of Transaction Costs]

21.17. Respondents were shown a typical SMS message displaying transaction values and related costs, like those used by financial service providers. Results showed that 72.6 per cent of respondents could accurately read and interpret a message indicating transaction costs on a mobile phone as shown in Figure 21.2.

[b) Knowledge of Transaction Costs by Education]

21.18. The survey results indicated that 81.0 per cent of the respondents who did not attend school could not read the SMS. Respondents with Tertiary level of education were able to read and interpret the SMS at 97.1 per cent, compared to only 9.3 per cent of respondents with no education (Figure 21.12).
heading_path: b) Knowledge of Transaction Costs by Education

text:
[Knowledge of Cost of Borrowing by Sex]

21.19. The survey assessed respondents' ability to accurately calculate 10.0 per cent interest on KSh 1,000 loan. Approximately 82.8 per cent of males correctly calculated the interest, compared to 77.5 per cent of females. Figure 21.13 shows that both sexes had improved knowledge of correctly calculating the interest.

[Climate Investments]

21.21. The survey findings, as shown in Figure 21.15, indicated that 34.9 per cent of the total population participated in various green environment initiatives. Key areas of investment in green initiatives included investing in solar-powered equipment and tree planting, whereby 18.8 per cent of the surveyed individuals cope with risks improved from 23.3 per cent in 2021 to 33.3 per cent in 2024, signaling better resilience.
